'''''Eucalyptus pulchella''''', commonly known as the '''white peppermint''' or '''narrow-leaved peppermint''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus pulchella'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_pulchella.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=30 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to Tasmania. it has smooth bark, sometimes with rough fibrous bark on older trees, linear leaves, flower buds in groups of nine to twenty or more, white flowers and cup-shaped to shortened spherical fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus pulchella'' is an erect tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|20|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth white or pale grey bark sometimes with rough, fibrous greyish bark on the trunk of older trees. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have narrow lance-shaped to linear leaves that are {{cvt|20-35|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-4|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are the same shade of glossy dark green on both sides, linear, {{cvt|33-120|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-10|mm}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|2-10|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of nine to twenty or more on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2-8|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-5|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to club-shaped, {{cvt|3-6|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-3|mm}} wide with a rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from November to March and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, cup-shaped to shortened spherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|4-6|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-7|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name=key>{{cite web| title=Key to Tasmanian Vascular Plants | year=2011 | url=http://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/MYRTS/sEucalyptus_pulchella.htm | last=Jordan | first=Greg | publisher=University of Tasmania}}</ref><ref name="Wiltshere">{{cite book|title=EucaFlip: Life-size guide to the eucalypts of Tasmania|year=2007|author1=Wiltshere, R.  |author2=Potts, B.}}</ref><ref>[http://www.apstas.com/White_peppermint.html The Unique Flora of Tasmania] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923172741/http://www.apstas.com/White_peppermint.html |date=2015-09-23 }}, Hobart District Group of The Australian Plants Society - Tasmania Inc.</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus pulchella'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20pulchella |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus pulchella'' was first formally described in 1829 by the [[botanist]] [[René Louiche Desfontaines]] in his book ''Catalogus Plantarum Horti Regii Parisiensis''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus pulchella''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455889|publisher=APNI|access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="Desf.">{{cite book |last1=Desfontaines |first1=René Louiche |title=Catalogus Plantarum Horti regii parisiensis cum annotationibus de plantis novis aut minus cognitis |date=1829 |publisher=J. S. Chaudé |location=Paris |page=408 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/137485#page/430/mode/1up |access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref> The [[Australian Plant Census]] lists the [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] as ''Eucalyptus linearis'', described in 1832 by [[Friedrich Dehnhardt]] in ''Catalogus Plantarum Horti Camaldulensis''<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus linearis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455163|publisher=APNI|access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref> and as ''Eucalyptus amygdalina'' var. ''angustifolia'' by [[Joseph Burtt Davy]] in ''Cyclopedia of American horticulture''<ref name=APNI2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus amygdalina'' var. ''angustifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455224|publisher=APNI|access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref> from an unpublished description by [[Ferdinand von Mueller]].<ref name="APC" /> The species name ''pulchella'' is a diminutive of the word pulcher which in [[Latin]] means beautiful. The common name, white peppermint, refers to its smooth white trunk.<ref name=names>{{cite book |author1=Wapstra, Mark |author2=Wapstra, Annie |author3=Wapstra, Hans | year=2010 | title=Tasmanian Plant Names Unravelled | pages=200–201 | location=Burwood, Victoria | publisher=Fullers Bookshop | isbn=978-09804720-2-8}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Eucalyptus pulchella'' is endemic to the lowlands of south-east Tasmania where it inhabits undulating, hilly terrain at altitudes between 100-500m above sea level.<ref name="Wiltshere"/> The interaction between [[Aspect (geography)|aspect]], soil type and water drainage play an important role in determining the distribution of ''E.pulchella''. It occurs on the upper north-west facing slopes of free-draining dolerite capped hills where soils are shallow. On such ridgetops water availability is limited due to the binding capacity of the Jurassic dolerite substrate and the shallow soil depth. Dry conditions due to the effect of soil are enhanced by aspect affect in which north-west facing slopes receive high solar insolation loads and are susceptible to periods of [[drought]] stress.<ref name=Williams1996/><ref name="Reid">{{cite book|title=Vegetation of Tasmania|year=1999|pages=198–223|author1=Reid, J.B.  |author2=Potts, B.M.|chapter=Eucalypt Biology}}</ref> The ability of ''E. pulchella'' to resist occasional severe drought explains its distribution on dry dolerite ridgetops. Although locally widespread ''E. pulchella'' is restricted to south-east Tasmania which may be explained by a glacial tree line preventing its spread into suitable habitats further north.<ref name=Kirkpatrick1987>{{cite journal |author1=Kirkpatrick, J.B.  |author2=Potts, B.M. | year=1987 | title=Isolated intermediates - product of long distance gene dispersal, phantom hybrids or convergent evolution? The case of the half barked ''Eucalyptus amygdalina'' | journal=Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania |volume=121 | pages=15–22|doi=10.26749/rstpp.121.15 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Although ''E. pulchella'' extends outside its range reaching as far north as [[Bothwell, Tasmania|Bothwell]], its true distribution is difficult to discern due to error involved with field identification due to a 'half barked' [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|intergrading]] form of ''[[Eucalyptus amygdalina]]''.<ref name=Kirkpatrick1987/>

''E. pulchella'' is a lowland [[species]] where it occurs on the upper slopes of well-drained sites with a [[Geology of Tasmania#Jurassic|Jurassic dolerite]] substrate in grassy or heathy open forests. Such sites typically have a north-west facing aspect with exposure to high solar insolation loads resulting in periodic drought stress.<ref name=Williams1996>{{cite journal |author1=Williams, K.J.  |author2=Potts, B.M. | year=1996 | title=The natural distribution of ''Eucalyptus'' species in Tasmania | journal=Tasforests |volume=8 | pages=39–149}}</ref>

''Eucalyptus pulchella'' occurs as a small to medium-sized spreading tree as the dominant species in grassy to heathy dry sclerophyll open forest and woodlands.<ref name=Williams1996/> Such dry sclerophyll communities have an open structure and rarely grow taller than 25m. The understory is typically dominated by the ground cover layer including native grasses and sedges such as ''[[Lomandra longifolia]]'' and is the most diverse. The shrub layer is sparse and typically includes species such as ''[[Exocarpos cupressiformis]]'' however, if the fire interval exceeds a 15-year interval the shrub may become dominant in the understory.<ref name="Kirkpatrick">{{cite book|title=Vegetation of Tasmania|year=1999|pages=198–223|author=Kirkpatrick, J.B.|chapter=Grassy Vegetation and Subalpine Eucalypt Communities}}</ref> ''E. pulchella'' is not always the dominant species, in sections of the east coast, hybrids between ''E. pulchella'' and ''E. amygdalina'' and genetic variants of ''E. amygdalina'' may act as the dominant species. ''Eucalyptus pulchella'' also commonly forms mixed stands with ''[[Eucalyptus globulus|E. globulus]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus viminalis|E. viminalis]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus rubida|E. rubida]]''.<ref name=Kitchener>{{cite book|author1=Kitchener, A.  |author2=Harris, S.|year=2013|title=From Forest to Fjaeldmark: Descriptions of Tasmania's Vegetation|edition=2|publisher=Department of Primary Industries, Parks, Water and Environment|location=Tasmania}}</ref>

==Ecology==

===Fire===
''Eucalyptus pulchella'' like many other species from the family Myrtaceae requires fire at least once in its lifetime to retain [[Ecological succession#Types of climax|disclimax]] vegetation and complete its lifecycle. Seeds of ''Eucalyptus'' are held in woody capsules which often remain on the tree for several years after reaching maturity. A fire event is required to dry out and open the woody capsule to release the seed. Fire creates a sterile, nutrient enriched ashbed which favours shade-intolerant eucalypt seedlings by eliminating any competitors.<ref name="Duncan">{{cite book|title=Vegetation of Tasmania|year=1999|pages=244–264|author=Duncan, F.|chapter=Dry Sclerophyll Forests and Woodlands}}</ref> In fact, dry sclerophyll communities and ''Eucalyptus'' species are fire promoting. The flammable nature of eucalypt bark and leaf litter which persists on the forest floor and the volatile oils in the leaves held in the canopy promote a fire frequency of approximately 20 years in dry sclerophyll communities.<ref name=Mount>{{cite journal | author=Mount, A.B. | year=1979 | title=Natural Regeneration Processes in Tasmanian Forests | journal=Search |volume=10 | pages=180–186}}</ref>

As well as seed regeneration, eucalypts utilise vegetative regeneration to recover from fire depending on its intensity. Eucalypts can do this by basal sprouting from lignotubers or from the stem, sprouting from epicormic buds.<ref name="Duncan"/>

===Pollination===
''Eucalyptus'' are preferential [[Outcrossing|outcrossers]] and production of seed is dependent on animal vectors to transfer [[pollen]] between flowers due to the unsuitability of the [[pollen]] to be transported by wind.<ref name=Hingston>{{cite journal |author1=Hingston, A.B.  |author2=Potts, B.M. | year=1998 | title=Floral visitors of ''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''globulus'' in eastern Tasmania | journal=Tasforests |volume=10 | pages=125–139}}</ref> [[Pollinator]]s are generally unspecific and tend to include both birds and insects which are attracted to the flower by a nectar reward. It is likely that pollen is transferred within a close proximity to its source due to the close to nearest-neighbour foraging pattern employed by birds. ''E. pulchella'' flowers at high intensity for approximately 2 months during summer reaching its peak around November.<ref name="Reid"/>

===Seed dispersal===
In ''Eucalyptus'' seed is housed in a woody capsule and is released through valves which open after the capsule has dried out. The capsules tend to be retained in the canopy for several years after reaching maturity. Seed is released on mass following a fire event or extremely hot weather conditions. Seed is typically dispersed one canopy height away from the base of the tree and apart from seed harvesting by [[ants]], movement is limited once it hits the ground.<ref name="Reid"/>
